title: Wild Australia · Episode 1
chapters: Platypus and echidnas: the egg-laying mammals

units.t: Wild Australia. Episode one.
In this episode: Marsupials: life in the pouch, Platypus and echidnas: the egg-laying mammals and Australia's remarkable birds.
Part one. Marsupials: life in the pouch.
Born the size of a jellybean, finished in a pouch.
Australia's marsupials took a very different path to the rest of the mammal world.
Born early.
A red kangaroo's pregnancy lasts only about 33 days.
The newborn joey is pink, hairless and under a gram, about the size of a jellybean.
Using its strong front legs, it crawls through its mother's fur to the pouch, latches onto a teat and stays for months.
That is the marsupial way: a short pregnancy with no long placental feeding, then development outside the body.
Some small species have no true pouch and carry young clinging underneath.
A mother kangaroo can pause a new embryo's development, called embryonic diapause, until the pouch is free.
She can also feed a joey at foot and a newborn at once, with two kinds of milk from two teats.
Of about 330 marsupial species, around two-thirds live in Australia and New Guinea.
Hopping kangaroos.
Kangaroos and wallabies are macropods, meaning 'big feet', a family of around 60 species.
The red kangaroo is the largest living marsupial; big males standing upright can be as tall as a person.
Hopping looks tiring, but long leg tendons store and release energy like springs, so once a kangaroo is moving, going faster costs surprisingly little extra effort.
Reds can briefly reach around 50 kilometres per hour.
Moving slowly, kangaroos use their strong tail as a fifth leg.
Kangaroos are most active around dawn and dusk, when collisions are most common, so take extra care driving then.
Koalas and wombats.
Koalas are not bears.
They eat almost only eucalyptus leaves, which are low in nutrients, high in fibre and toxic to most animals.
A long gut and specialised microbes help, and young koalas eat a soft faeces called pap from their mother to gain those microbes.
The diet gives so little energy that koalas rest or sleep 18 to 22 hours a day.
In 2022, koalas in Queensland, New South Wales and the ACT were listed as endangered, mainly through habitat loss, disease, dogs and cars.
Wombats are the only animals known to make cube-shaped poo, dozens of cubes a night, left on rocks and logs as territory markers.
A 2018 study found that regions of differing stiffness in the last stretch of intestine shape the drying droppings.
It won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2019.
Devils and the tiger.
The Tasmanian devil is the largest living carnivorous marsupial, with one of the most powerful bites for its size of any mammal.
Devils vanished from the mainland about 3,000 years ago.
Since the mid-1990s, devil facial tumour disease, a rare cancer spread by biting, has caused severe declines.
Insurance populations are bred in captivity, and since 2020 some devils have been released into a fenced sanctuary in New South Wales.
The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was the largest carnivorous marsupial of modern times, a dog-like hunter with dark stripes across its back.
Seen as a threat to sheep, it was targeted by a government bounty from 1888 to 1909, with more than 2,000 paid.
The last known thylacine died at Beaumaris Zoo, Hobart, on 7 September 1936, now National Threatened Species Day.
Why Australia.
Australia's marsupial richness is a story of isolation.
After Australia separated from Antarctica tens of millions of years ago and drifted north, its marsupials evolved on their own, filling roles that placental mammals fill elsewhere.
The results show striking convergent evolution: sugar gliders resemble flying squirrels, the marsupial mole resembles golden moles, and the thylacine looked remarkably like a wolf.
The practical side is simple.
Drive slowly at dawn and dusk in the bush.
If you find an injured animal, or a dead kangaroo or wombat by the road, call a local wildlife rescue service, because a living joey may still be in the pouch.
The key idea: Marsupials give birth to tiny, barely formed young that finish developing attached to a teat, usually in a pouch.
Part two. Platypus and echidnas: the egg-laying mammals.
When the first platypus reached Britain, scientists checked it for stitches.
It was real, and it was even stranger than it looked.
Five egg-laying species.
Only five living mammal species lay eggs: the platypus and four species of echidna.
Together they are the monotremes, a group that split from the ancestors of all other mammals more than 160 million years ago.
The name means 'single opening': like birds and reptiles, they have one opening, the cloaca, for waste and reproduction.
The platypus lives only in eastern Australia, including Tasmania.
The short-beaked echidna lives across Australia and New Guinea, while the three long-beaked echidnas live only in New Guinea.
They are not 'primitive' leftovers but highly specialised animals with a very long, separate evolutionary history.
Fur, milk and eggs.
Monotremes have fur, a single lower jawbone and the three tiny middle ear bones typical of mammals, and they feed their young on milk.
The twist: they have no nipples.
Milk seeps out through pores on patches of belly skin, and the young lick or suck it up.
They are warm-blooded but run cooler than most mammals, at around 32 degrees Celsius compared with our 37.
Adult platypuses have no teeth and grind food with hard pads; echidnas never have teeth.
A female platypus seals herself in a riverbank burrow and incubates one to three soft, leathery eggs for roughly ten days.
An echidna lays one egg into a temporary belly pouch.
It hatches after about ten days, and the baby, called a puggle, stays until its spines begin to grow.
Bill and spur.
The platypus bill is soft, rubbery and packed with sensors.
Diving, the platypus closes its eyes, ears and nostrils, so it hunts almost blind.
Tens of thousands of electroreceptors detect the faint electric fields from prey muscles, and touch receptors help too.
Sweeping its head side to side, it finds larvae, worms and yabbies in the mud, stores them in cheek pouches and chews at the surface.
Males carry a sharp spur on each hind ankle, joined to a venom gland.
Venom production rises in the breeding season, which suggests it is mainly used in fights between males.
A spur injury isn't known to be fatal to humans but causes severe pain and swelling that ordinary painkillers barely touch, sometimes for weeks.
Never handle a wild platypus.
The echidna.
The short-beaked echidna lives in almost every habitat in Australia, from deserts and forests to the snowy high country, making it the most widespread native mammal on the continent.
Its spines are modified hairs.
It laps up ants and termites with a long, sticky tongue, and its snout carries electroreceptors too, though far fewer than a platypus bill.
When threatened, an echidna digs straight down or curls into a spiky ball.
In winter, several males sometimes follow a female in a line called an 'echidna train'.
Male echidnas also have ankle spurs, but they don't deliver venom; a gland on the spur appears to produce a secretion in the breeding season, possibly for communication.
Echidnas are long-lived for their size, surviving for decades.
Doubted, now threatened.
First Nations peoples had known these animals for tens of thousands of years, but European naturalists were baffled.
When a preserved platypus reached Britain in the late 1790s, George Shaw, who described it in 1799, wondered if it was a fake, a duck's bill stitched onto a mammal.
Scientists argued for decades over whether monotremes laid eggs, as Aboriginal informants said.
In 1884, William Caldwell, working in Queensland, found proof and telegraphed that they were 'oviparous', or egg-laying.
Today the platypus is listed as Near Threatened globally.
Threats include dams, drought, land clearing, pollution, foxes, dogs and drowning in enclosed yabby traps, banned in several states.
To see one, visit a quiet creek at dawn or dusk, stay still and watch for ripples.
Pick up fishing line and hair ties.
The key idea: Only five living mammals lay eggs, and they are specialised animals, not primitive leftovers.
Part three. Australia's remarkable birds.
Nearly half the world's bird species descend from ancestors that sang in ancient Australia.
The birds here are older, louder and cleverer than you might think.
Where song began.
Songbirds, including robins, finches, crows and sparrows, number roughly 5,000 species, close to half of all birds.
Scientists long assumed they began in the Northern Hemisphere.
DNA studies from the early 2000s showed the oldest songbird lineages, including lyrebirds, scrub-birds, bowerbirds and treecreepers, live in Australia and New Guinea.
The strong consensus is that songbirds evolved here tens of millions of years ago, then spread worldwide.
So a European blackbird singing in London carries an Australian inheritance.
The superb lyrebird takes song to an extreme.
A male's song is largely near-perfect copies of kookaburras, whipbirds and rosellas, woven with his own calls as he displays his lacy tail.
Some captive birds have copied camera shutters and machinery.
Clever, social birds.
Australia has more than 50 parrot species, including cockatoos, galahs, lorikeets and budgerigars.
Cockatoos are exceptionally intelligent and long-lived: Cookie, a Major Mitchell's cockatoo, reached about 83 in a US zoo.
In Sydney, sulphur-crested cockatoos learned to lift wheelie-bin lids.
A 2021 study tracked the skill spreading across suburbs as birds learned by watching, a rare example of animal culture in a city.
Residents respond with bricks and gadgets, and the birds keep testing them.
Australian magpies are closer to butcherbirds than to European magpies.
They live in cooperative family groups and sing together to announce territory.
In a 2022 study, magpies fitted with tracking harnesses were apparently helped out of them by others.
Swooping happens in spring and only some males do it; calmly walk away.
Emus and cassowaries.
The emu is the world's second-tallest bird after the ostrich, up to about 1.
9 metres.
It can't fly but runs at around 50 kilometres per hour and swims well.
The female lays large, dark green eggs, then often leaves.
The male incubates them for about eight weeks, barely eating or drinking, then guards the striped chicks for months.
The emu and the kangaroo appear on Australia's coat of arms.
The southern cassowary, Australia's heaviest bird, lives in far north Queensland rainforest, with a helmet-like casque and a dagger-like claw on each foot.
It swallows fruit whole and passes the seeds intact, often far away, so some rainforest plants rely on it.
The Australian population is endangered.
Cassowaries are shy but can kick hard when cornered or fed.
Never feed one.
The Emu War.
In late 1932, a large number of emus, often estimated at around 20,000, moved onto wheat farms in Western Australia's Campion district.
Farmers, many of them former soldiers, asked the federal government for help.
Defence Minister George Pearce sent Major G.
P.
W.
Meredith with a small group of soldiers, two Lewis machine guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition.
The emus scattered into small groups, ran fast and proved very hard to hit.
After two attempts, the military withdrew.
Meredith claimed 986 kills for 9,860 rounds fired, a figure historians treat cautiously.
Later bounty schemes and better fencing did more to protect crops.
The 'war' became a famous piece of Australian folklore.
Enjoying birds wisely.
More than 800 bird species have been recorded in Australia, and a large share are found nowhere else.
You don't need to travel to enjoy them: a local park, wetland or backyard can host dozens.
Taking part in citizen science, such as BirdLife Australia's Aussie Backyard Bird Count each October, turns your observations into useful data.
To help birds, plant local native shrubs that provide food and shelter, offer a shallow bird bath with clean water and keep cats indoors, especially at night.
Avoid feeding wild birds bread or mince, which can make them sick and create dependence.
A pair of binoculars and a field guide app go a long way.
The key idea: Songbirds, nearly half of all birds, first evolved in Australia and New Guinea.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. How do marsupials differ from other mammals in reproduction?
Answer. A short pregnancy, then a tiny newborn on a teat.
Question two. Which statement about monotremes is correct?
Answer. They are specialised, with a long separate history.
Question three. Why does a European blackbird carry an 'Australian inheritance'?
Answer. Songbirds first evolved here, then spread.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
